title: Preserve tibbles in lmap()
description:
`lmap()`, `lmap_at()` and `lmap_if()` documented that they return a data frame "matching `.x`", but a tibble input came back as a plain `data.frame` because each piece went through `as.data.frame()` before `list_cbind()`. The result is now restored to the class of `.x` with `vec_restore()` when `.x` is a tibble, as `modify()` already does.

``` r
tibble::as_tibble(iris) |> lmap(identity) |> class()
#> before: "data.frame"
#> after:  "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame"
```

Plain data frames and data.tables are unchanged. Values, names and row counts are identical to before for all tibble inputs I compared.

Closes #1051

title: Rewrite `reduce()` and family in C
description:
Closes #1168 and closes #1243. Your acceptation of #1169 prompted me to tackle a bigger task 🦔 

This PR reimplements `reduce()` (and `reduce2()`, `accumulate()`, and `accumulate2()` as well) in C. The idea came from Hadley's comment on #1168 stating that it'd be hard to performantly add progress bars to `reduce()` as they are written in C, so I rewrote the function in C instead. It is more performant too, getting `reduce()` to be on par with base `Reduce()`:

``` r
x <- as.list(1:20000)
# Without .init or .progress
bench::mark(
  purrr::reduce_old(x, sum),
  purrr::reduce(x, sum),
  Reduce(sum, x),
  min_time = 1
)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   expression                     min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 purrr::reduce_old(x, sum)   15.1ms  15.37ms      61.9     762KB     81.8
#> 2 purrr::reduce(x, sum)       8.08ms   8.35ms     118.      170KB     73.6
#> 3 Reduce(sum, x)              7.72ms   8.05ms     124.      349KB     51.6
```

<sup>Created on 2026-01-18 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

`accumulate()` isn't quite as fast as in base R, but there's improvement nonetheless:

``` r
x <- as.list(1:20000)
bench::mark(
  purrr::accumulate_old(x, sum, .init = 0),
  purrr::accumulate(x, sum, .init = 0),
  Reduce(sum, x, init = 0, accumulate = TRUE),
  min_time = 1
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression                            min  median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                        <bch:t> <bch:t>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 purrr::accumulate_old(x, sum, .i… 26.2ms  27.3ms       36.8    1.45MB    178. 
#> 2 purrr::accumulate(x, sum, .init … 12.92ms 14.14ms      69.7    1.47MB    103. 
#> 3 Reduce(sum, x, init = 0, accumul…  9.33ms  9.86ms     100.   505.53KB     73.1
```

<sup>Created on 2026-01-28 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I tried not to change any behavior (except for #1243) and hopefully succeeded, though that meant adding a lot of tests in the end. That was also the reason I didn't tackle #1245, as it'd change non-erroring behavior.

As for the code, well... It's not pretty, but I couldn't think of any approach that would look cleaner with interacting `.init`, `.dir`, and `done()`, and trying to make one shared implementation for all four functions with only some differences in certain points of the algorithm. If you prefer, I can separate C loops for `reduce()` and `accumulate()` family, that would probably be the most influential one. If I were to say, it's probably 15-20% more complex than the current R implementation (numbers completely made-up).

Finally, the C implementation should make it very easy to add `.dir` parameter to `reduce2()` and `accumulate2()`, as well as make `accumulate2()` return a named vector if input is named, like `accumulate()` does. Then again, I didn't want to add more changes than necessary and I can always add it later if you so wish.

No worries, I'm quickly running out of purrr functions to optimize :)

title: Optimize `detect_index()` and derivatives
description:
I saw `as_predicate()` + `for`-loop, I had to have a go at it 🦔 

I rewrote `detect_index()` as `which_satisfies_predicate()` in C. It's very similar to `satisfies_predicate()` powering `every()` and friends, and at one point I thought about making one shared implementation for these, as both these families look for the first element that behaves differently to the previous ones in a predicate. I'd just change `every()` and friends to test the index against 0.

However, the differences were too numerous:
* `detect_index()` doesn't allow `NA`, while `every()` propagates it;
* `detect_index()` allows setting backward direction, while `every()` doesn't;
* `detect_index()` names its predicate parameter `.f` (historical leftover, I assume), while `every()` has `.p`.

Therefore, I kept them separate. Also, regarding the last point, I had to handle that anyway due to `head_while()` and `tail_while()` having `.p` as well.

There's a lot of ideas shared with `every()` in R as well, `which_satisfies_predicate()` in R follows very similar logic as `satisfies_predicate()`, replacing `as_predicate()` with `as_mapper()` and performing bool check in R in particular. This bool check doesn't test for attributes nor classes, just like the analogous scalar logical check in `every()`.

You will see the `.negate` argument to `which_satisfies_predicate()`. The reason for that is for optimal handling of `head_while()` and `tail_while()` which look for the first element _not_ satisfying a predicate. They had `negate(as_predicate())` before, but that was _very_ costly (you'll see how much in the benchmark) and had to go. But I couldn't (obviously) negate `.p` directly, and the `as_mapper()` call only took part inside `which_satisfies_predicate()`, so... I moved it completely inside C, so that there's even less overhead.

Most test cases were adapted from `every()`, so that they should cover most weird inputs in here as well.

----

As for the reason for this C rewrite - `detect_index()` and `detect()` are now about three times faster:

``` r
cross::bench_branches({
  x <- 5e5:-1
  is_negative <- \(x) x < 0
  
  bench::mark(purrr::detect_index(x, is_negative), iterations = 10)
})
#> # A tibble: 2 × 14
#>   branch  expression   min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr  n_gc total_time result memory     time      
#>   <chr>   <bch:expr> <bch> <bch:>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl> <int> <dbl>   <bch:tm> <list> <list>     <list>    
#> 1 optimi… purrr::de… 249ms  286ms      3.48     733KB     50.4    10   145      2.88s <int>  <Rprofmem> <bench_tm>
#> 2 main    purrr::de… 777ms  842ms      1.19     797KB     30.5    10   257      8.43s <int>  <Rprofmem> <bench_tm>
# ℹ 1 more variable: gc <list>

cross::bench_branches({
  x <- 5e5:-1
  is_negative <- \(x) x < 0
  
  bench::mark(purrr::detect(x, is_negative), iterations = 10)
})
#> # A tibble: 2 × 14
#>   branch  expression   min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr  n_gc total_time result memory     time      
#>   <chr>   <bch:expr> <bch> <bch:>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl> <int> <dbl>   <bch:tm> <list> <list>     <list>    
#> 1 optimi… purrr::de… 246ms  300ms      3.50     735KB     50.8    10   145      2.85s <int>  <Rprofmem> <bench_tm>
#> 2 main    purrr::de… 791ms  824ms      1.21     797KB     31.0    10   257       8.3s <int>  <Rprofmem> <bench_tm>
# ℹ 1 more variable: gc <list>
```

<sup>Created on 2026-02-03 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

The real difference is in `head_while()` and `tail_while()`, though. The first time I ran the benchmark, I went to fix the number of iterations, because I thought I rolled a very slow execution of the current implementation. I expected a speedup factor of three, like above, but instead, I got 25:

``` r
cross::bench_branches({
  x <- 2e5:-1
  is_positive <- \(x) x > 0
  
  bench::mark(purrr::head_while(x, is_positive), iterations = 10)
})
#> # A tibble: 2 × 14
```

title: Add `.progress` to `map_if()`, `modify_if()`, `modify_at()`, and the `lmap()` family
description:
🤖 Written by AI 🤖

Each of these functions now shows a single progress bar spanning all of its phases (e.g. predicate + transformation in `map_if()`). Progress bars are now created on the R side by `as_progress()` and ticked directly by the C mapping loop, which means the vendored cleancall could be removed.

The R-to-C handoff of the cli bar object is a hack pending https://github.com/r-lib/cli/issues/850; parallel maps via mirai reject shared bars pending https://github.com/r-lib/mirai/issues/663.

title: Simpler and more performant handling of `R_MissingArg`
description:
Merges into #1276 as an alternative approach

We bind `.x_i` and friends as a forced promise whose value is `R_MissingArg`. This means it can be "evaluated" like normal, and returns `R_MissingArg` as people expect.

This is much simpler than adjusting the call itself, and avoids overhead of `PROTECT()` / `UNPROTECT()` in the normal path, and allocations in the missing path.

title: Fix named-list `.progress` with `in_parallel()`
description:
🤖 Written by AI 🤖

Fixes #1253. With daemons set, a named-list `.progress` failed because `as_progress()` injects a `caller` element that mirai forwarded to `cli::cli_progress_bar()`, which has no such argument. `mmap_()` now strips it, and errors raised while collecting parallel results keep their original message instead of the empty `In index: .`.

title: Document exactly what map() and friends pass to .f
description:
🤖 Written by AI 🤖

Adds @details sections to map(), map2(), pmap(), keep(), and detect() stating the exact call form of .f (e.g. .f(.x[[1]], ...), .f(.x[[2]], ...), ...), that [[ subsetting is used, and that names are not passed.

Fixes #1273

title: Don't use formulas
description:
🤖 Written by AI 🤖

Formulas like `~ .x + 1` in place of functions are now soft-deprecated in favor of anonymous functions (`\(x) x + 1`). Also threads the user's environment through `as_mapper()` for correct package attribution in the lifecycle footer, and simplifies `as_predicate()` by dropping its `.mapper` argument (callers now call `as_mapper()` themselves).

Fixes #1280

title: Implement `compose()` lazily
description:
Fixes #651 🦔 

I simplified the code a bit by making the `composed()` function simply construct the `f3(f2(f1(...)))` call iteratively with `rlang::call2()` (my beloved) and only then evaluate it. Kind of wanted to use `reduce()` here, but there were interactions that made it not compose lazily, so an old `for` loop it is then.

Technically, it should be possible to move most of that call creation outside of `composed()` function for potential performance gains (i.e. have a predefined `f3(f2(f1()))` call in the outer env and only insert parameters and evaluate during the actual call), but I can't see an easy way to do it right now.

~As with #1246, the last commit contains updated snaps for vctrs v0.7.0.~

Fixes #1243. Fixes #1245. Closes #1260.

title: Fix global variable NOTE for crated `f` in `compact()`
description:
This NOTE came up when I ran R CMD check for #1282: `no visible global function definition for 'f'`.

The NOTE comes from the crated predicate in `compact()` (#1279). The crate bundles `f` through `crate_fn()`, but codetools cannot see this. This PR declares `f` with `utils::globalVariables()`, the same approach as the existing `!<-` declaration in `adverb-partial.R`.

title: Support `in_parallel()` predicates in `keep()` and friends
description:
🤖 Written by AI 🤖

`as_predicate()` wrapped every predicate in a plain closure, stripping the crate class from `in_parallel()` functions so they silently ran sequentially. It now returns crated predicates untouched, so `keep()`, `discard()`, `map_if()`, `modify_if()`, and `lmap_if()` evaluate their predicates in parallel when daemons are set.

Fixes #1252.

title: Move mirai and carrier to Imports
description:
Closes #1231, closes #1233.

mirai (>= 2.5.1) and carrier (>= 0.4.0) move from Suggests to Imports, so `in_parallel()` works out of the box. This removes the runtime package checks, test skips, and conditional examples that guarded against their absence.

title: Fix mapping over missing arguments
description:
🤖 Written by AI 🤖

#1263 changed the `map()` family to bind each element to a variable (`.x_i`, `.y_i`, `.l_{j}_i`) and call `.f(.x_i)`, instead of passing the lazy expression `.x[[i]]`. When an element is the missing argument (the empty symbol, `quote(expr = )`), binding it to `.x_i` makes `.x_i` itself a missing variable, so evaluating the argument fails:

```r
x <- list(a = quote(expr = ), b = 1)
purrr::map_lgl(x, is.name)
#> Error in `map_lgl()`:
#> ℹ In index: 1.
#> Caused by error in `map_()`:
#> ! argument ".x_i" is missing, with no default
```

The missing argument ends up in lists more often than you might expect, typically when introspecting function arguments:

* `formals()` of a function with arguments that have no default, e.g. admiral finds mandatory arguments with `formals(derivation) |> keep(is_missing)`; broom/modeltests do `map_lgl(formals(f), is.name)`.
* `as.list(environment())` inside a function whose arguments weren't supplied, e.g. hypothesis does `environment() |> as.list() |> keep(~ !is.symbol(.x))` to drop unsupplied args.
* `rlang::env_get_list()` on the calling environment, e.g. gtexr collects query parameters this way, then `map()`s over them.
* Captured empty `[` indices like `x[, 1]`, e.g. dibble `map2()`s over the dimension names and the indices.

This broke 19 revdeps (#1275). Putting `R_MissingArg` directly in the call doesn't work either, since R then treats the argument as not supplied. Instead, only for elements that are the missing argument, we pass `quote(<missing>)`, which evaluates to the missing argument as an ordinary value. The fast path is unchanged for everything else.

title: Add explicit parameters wherever necessary
description:
~~This is a draft, as I'm both waiting to see if I covered all possibilities and unsure if I'm not starting too many PRs at once.~~

Closes three small and related issues 🦔 

Closes #1244: `.ptype` is now explicitly stated for `imap_vec()`. Couldn't think of a test case.

Closes #1249: `.progress` is now explicitly stated for `keep()`, `discard()`, `modify()`, `modify2()`, and `imodify()`. Moreover, `compact()` gained one as well. I'm on the fence regarding `map_if()` and `modify_if()`, since these two functions may spawn two progress bars if `.else` is specified. I don't want to allow it like that, but also I don't want to forbid it, as some people may be using it. I might do a C rewrite one day that would handle it better than R code could.

Closes #1248: Many internal parameters are now passed named. These names were added whenever there were `...` upstream that could take that parameter and pass it down without it being consumed anywhere. Now, whenever the user passes, say, `.else` to `lmap_at()`, they will get an error stating that that formal argument was matched by more than one actual argument. While the error could be a bit more clear, it should be an upgrade over the current state where the user would usually get errors related to mismatching types of different arguments due to them oftentimes being pushed down by that user-added argument. Or, occassionally, not get an error at all. This one got a few test cases to cover some of the possible parameter names that a given function shouldn't allow in `...`.

title: Pass user_env to vctrs compat helpers in pmap()
description:
# Pass user_env to vctrs compat helpers in pmap()

`pmap_()` in R/pmap.R calls `vctrs_list_compat()` and `vctrs_vec_compat()` without their `user_env` argument. Both helpers live in R/utils.R and take `user_env` as a required formal; they hand it to `lifecycle::deprecate_soft()` when the input is a pairlist. So any pairlist passed to `pmap()` fails before the deprecation warning can fire:

```r
pmap(pairlist(1:2, 3:4), sum)
#> Error: argument "user_env" is missing, with no default
```

Found during my most recent [ry](https://github.com/sims1253/ry) audit.

title: (2) Rework `map()` family internals for performance
description:
Branched from https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/pull/1263

(I was dumb and opened #1263 from my personal fork, so I can't make the base branch of this PR the other PR and still have it open on `tidyverse/purrr`. I'll rebase on `main` after we merge that one and then the minimal diff becomes clear)

Pulls the best idea out of https://github.com/DavisVaughan/purrr/pull/1, which is to construct calls of `.f(.x)` rather than `.f(.x, ...)` when there are no `...` provided by the user. Surprisingly this ends up having ~10% less overhead in the primitive function case, like with `names`. But the improvements quickly get lost in the noise with more expensive functions.

title: Rework `map()` family internals for performance
description: Closes https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/pull/1255 with an alternative design, but a similar approach @ErdaradunGaztea had some really nice ideas outlined in #1255. Using C level accessors for unclassed objects in `map()` is also something I've been wanting to work on for awhile, so that was a nice jumping off point that proved out the concept. I've taken that PR to its extreme, rewriting to match our style a bit more, and also extending support to `pmap()`. # Overview! This PR rewrites the guts of `map()`, `map2()`, and `pmap()` (and thus, the whole family really). The core change was to recognize that we were adding quite a bit of overhead by accessing elements with `[[` like this: ```r # map() .f(.x[[i]], ...) # map2() .f(.x[[i]], .y[[i]], ...) # pmap() .f(.l[[1]][[i]], .l[[2]][[i]], .l[[3]][[i]], ...) ``` For unclassed objects, extracting with `[[` adds a rather large amount of overhead! Particularly with large lists if your `.f` is extremely fast, like with `names()` or `is.null()`. Also, for `pmap()` in particular it's pretty wasteful to do `.l[[1]]` at each iteration! We actually know `.l` is a bare list at that point, so we can extract that once up front. Instead, we can do this with unclassed objects (enjoy my pseudo C / R code): ```r v_x <- VECTOR_PTR_RO(x) # done once up front .x_i <- v_x[i] # at each iteration, fast C access and Rf_defineVar to bind to `.x_i` .f(.x_i, ...) # now call this instead v_x <- VECTOR_PTR_RO(x) v_y <- VECTOR_PTR_RO(y) .x_i <- v_x[i] .y_i <- v_y[i] .f(.x_i, .y_i, ...) v_l <- VECTOR_PTR_RO(l) v_l_1 <- VECTOR_PTR_RO(v_l[1]) v_l_2 <- VECTOR_PTR_RO(v_l[2]) v_l_3 <- VECTOR_PTR_RO(v_l[3]) # all this is done up front! .l_1_i <- v_l_1[i] .l_2_i <- v_l_2[i] .l_3_i <- v_l_3[i] .f(l_1_i, l_2_i, .l_3_i, ...) ``` And with classed objects, we still make the `.x_i` binding, we just do it via `[[` like before. For unclassed objects, this does significantly reduce the amount of overhead that purrr itself is adding on top of user function execution (see benchmarks). The challenge of this PR was doing this in a clean way, but I think I've managed something that feels pretty good, symmetrical, and maintainable across all of map/map2/pmap. # Breaking change-ish Technically the call we create for `.f` is different now, i.e. ``` r library(purrr) map(1, function(x) sys.call()) #> [[1]] #> .f(.x[[i]], ...) map(1, function(x) substitute(x)) #> [[1]] #> .x[[i]] ``` After: ``` r library(purrr) map(1, function(x) sys.call()) #> [[1]] #> .f(.x_i, ...) map(1, function(x) substitute(x)) #> [[1]] #> .x_i ``` I would hope that no one is actually relying on this (beyond a single one of our own tests). And if someone accidentally was, then I think I would be happy to send them a PR to fix this, because this feels like "purrr internals" territory. Note that this call does _not_ show up in a standard error report: ``` r purrr::map(1, function(x) x + "i") #> Error in `purrr::map()`: #> ℹ In index: 1. #> Caused by error in `x + "i"`: #> ! non-numeric argument to binary operator ``` It does show up in the traceback (both rlang's and `traceback()`) but it is in there pretty deep in "internals" territory IMO, so this doesn't bother me, and I still think it is reasonably informative: # Benchmarks! A handful of benchmarks are listed below. Somewhat arbitrary, but I do think patterns like `map(x, names)` and `map_lgl(x, is.null)` in particular are pretty common, and since `.f` is a primitive that is already extremely fast, a large part of the overhead here was actually us and the way we accessed elements of `.x`. Also, not shown here, but you can treat "old purrr" as roughly equivalent to base `lapply()` and friends. So we have gotten faster than `lapply()` with many common cases, which is cool! ```r # map # Pluck names off each list element # - Large unclassed list (uses `VECTOR_PTR_RO`) # - map() # - primitive names() cross::bench_versions( pkgs = c("DavisVaughan/purrr@feature/faster-map", "purrr"), { library(purrr) x <- as.list(1:1e6 + 0L) bench::mark(map(x, names), iterations = 50) } ) #> # A tibble: 2 × 7 #> pkg expression min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` #> #> 1 DavisVaughan/purrr@fe… map(x, na… 59.3ms 60.8ms 16.2 7.82MB 22.4 #> 2 purrr map(x, na… 129.4ms 136.6ms 7.00 7.82MB 11.8 # Slightly slower when we have classed objects, but typically a custom `[[` # method is going to dominate the computation anyways # - Large classed list (we use `[[`) # - map() # - primitive names() cross::bench_versions( pkgs = c("DavisVaughan/purrr@feature/faster-map", "purrr"), { library(purrr) x <- structure(as.list(1:1e6 + 0L), class = c("foo", "list")) bench::mark(map(x, names), iterations = 50) } ) #> # A tibble: 2 × 7 #> pkg expression min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` #> #> 1 DavisVaughan/purrr@featu… map(x, na… 563ms 583ms 1.68 7.82MB 10.4 #> 2 purrr map(x, na… 539ms 557ms 1.77 7.82MB 10.9 # - Many columned data.frame (special case, we unclass this internally already # in vctrs_vec_compat so we end up using fast VECTOR_PTR_RO) # - map_chr # - primitive typeof cross::bench_versions( pkgs = c("DavisVaughan/purrr@feature/faster-map", "purrr"), { library(purrr) names <- as.character(1:1e5) x <- vctrs::new_data_frame(rlang::set_names(as.list(1:1e5 + 0L), names)) bench::mark(map_chr(x, typeof), iterations = 50) } ) #> # A tibble: 2 × 7 #> pkg expression min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` #> #> 1 DavisVaughan/purrr@feat… map_chr(x… 17.8ms 18.7ms 50.9 945KB 181. #> 2 purrr map_chr(x… 26.5ms 27.5ms 35.8 945KB 36.5 # Detect `NULL`s # - Large unclassed list # - map_lgl() # - primitive is.null() cross::bench_versions( pkgs = c("DavisVaughan/purrr@feature/faster-map", "purrr"), { library(purrr) set.seed(123) x <- sample(list(NULL, 1), 1e6, replace = TRUE) bench::mark(map_lgl(x, is.null), iterations = 50) } ) #> # A tibble: 2 × 7 #> pkg expression min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` #> #> 1 DavisVaughan/purrr@fe… map_lgl(x… 65.4ms 68.9ms 14.2 4MB 66.0 #> 2 purrr map_lgl(x… 134.7ms 142.3ms 6.92 4MB 52.3 # Just showing iteration over an atomic # - Large unclassed atomic (use `INTEGER_RO`, etc) # - map_int() # - non-primitive identity(), so slower in general cross::bench_versions( pkgs = c("DavisVaughan/purrr@feature/faster-map", "purrr"), { library(purrr) x <- 1:1e6 + 0L bench::mark(map_int(x, identity), iterations = 50) } ) #> # A tibble: 2 × 7 #> pkg expression min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` #> #> 1 DavisVaughan/purrr@featu… map_int(x… 167ms 176ms 5.62 3.97MB 59.2 #> 2 purrr map_int(x… 234ms 247ms 4.02 3.97MB 54.2 ``` ```r # map2 # Set an attribute on each element # - Large unclassed list # - Large unclassed integer # - map2() # - primitive `attr<-`() cross::bench_versions( pkgs = c("DavisVaughan/purrr@feature/faster-map", "purrr"), { library(purrr) set.seed(123) x <- as.list(1:1e6 + 0L) y <- sample(letters, 1e6, replace = TRUE) bench::mark( map2(x, y, `attr<-`, which = "y"), iterations = 50 ) } ) #> # A tibble: 2 × 7 #> pkg expression min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` #> #> 1 DavisVaughan/purrr@feat… "map2(x, … 484ms 752.6ms 1.23 7.79MB 3.62 #> 2 purrr "map2(x, … 488ms 1.15s 0.889 7.78MB 4.27 # Two classed atomics (So these access with `[[`, and use a real custom method, # which dominates the time here) cross::bench_versions( pkgs = c("DavisVaughan/purrr@feature/faster-map", "purrr"), { library(purrr) set.seed(123) x <- .Date(sample(1:10, 1e6, replace = TRUE)) y <- .Date(sample(1:10, 1e6, replace = TRUE)) bench::mark(map2(x, y, list), iterations = 5) } ) #> # A tibble: 2 × 7 #> pkg expression min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` #> #> 1 DavisVaughan/purrr@featu… map2(x, y… 5.32s 5.37s 0.180 38.3MB 4.46 #> 2 purrr map2(x, y… 5.26s 5.41s 0.181 38.3MB 4.48 ``` ```r # pmap # Poor man's transpose-ish operation # - Large unclassed atomics # - pmap() # - primitive list cross::bench_versions( pkgs = c("DavisVaughan/purrr@feature/faster-map", "purrr"), { library(purrr) set.seed(123) x <- sample(1:10, 1e6, replace = TRUE) y <- sample(letters, 1e6, replace = TRUE) z <- sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 1e6, replace = TRUE) bench::mark(pmap(list(x, y, z), list), iterations = 50) } ) #> # A tibble: 2 × 7 #> pkg expression min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` #> #> 1 DavisVaughan/purrr@featu… pmap(list… 337ms 407ms 2.52 7.87MB 6.99 #> 2 purrr pmap(list… 646ms 855ms 1.20 7.87MB 5.53 # - title: Speed up `map()` and `map2()` somewhat (~20%?)
description:
Hi, I'd like to propose a way to speed `map()` and `map2()` up by... well, that's difficult to tell, but 20% seems to be a solid guess.

So, I've noticed that `pluck()` has a very interesting implementation of `extract_vector()` where it'd first try to extract the vector element using C API and only dispatch to `[[` when the variable is an object (with classes). Since `map()` already drops classes from lists unless they are vectors as understood by {vctrs} (so very rarely), I figured it'd make sense to split `map()` implementation into two, keeping current behaviour for objects, but optimizing it akin to `pluck()` for everything else.

Currently, `map()` executes a call of the form `.f(.x[[i]], ...)` (or `.f(.x[[i]], .y[[i]], ...)`, but I'm gonna skip `map2()` for now) in each iteration. It'd be better if we could pass `i`-th element of `.x` to `.f()` instead, i.e. `.f(value, ...)`, where `value` was extracted in C. This would, however, require re-creating a call each time - though that was still faster overall - and makes the code stray further from the original implementation that we still keep for the classed object case. And I wanted to add as little code as possible.

So, I've decided to add an `.x_i` object on R side and make C assign to it upon calculating `value`. Now it's a simple `.f(.x_i, ...)` call that can be defined once, and the logic is very similar. There's an extra call to an `r_extractor` object that is also a new parameter to the mapping loop. Oh, and `x` and `y` are also passed to C now, as we need to extract from them now. That doesn't seem to be much of a cost, though.

What else? I've extracted call creation to a separate file, `calls.c`, because there are four calls now instead of two for `map()` and `map2()`. I've skipped one test case that tested internal implementation too much but added a new one too.

Also, a benchmark:

(Using base R `lapply()` and `mapply()` as benchmark, as `cross::bench_branches()` doesn't work with `reprex()`; their performance is pretty much equal to that of purrr v1.2.1, though)

``` r
x <- 0:1e5
bench::mark(
  purrr = purrr::map(x, \(x) sqrt(x)),
  base = lapply(x, \(x) sqrt(x)),
  iterations = 20
)
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is
#> disabled.
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 purrr        40.2ms   50.5ms      18.3     5.8MB     22.9
#> 2 base         53.2ms   78.2ms      11.3   781.3KB     17.5
```

<sup>Created on 2026-03-20 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

``` r
x <- 0:1e5
y <- 1e5:2e5
bench::mark(
  purrr = purrr::map2(x, y, \(x, y) sqrt(y) - sqrt(x)),
  base = mapply(
    \(x, y) sqrt(y) - sqrt(x),
    x, y,
    SIMPLIFY = FALSE, USE.NAMES = FALSE
  ),
  iterations = 15
)
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is
#> disabled.
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 purrr        64.2ms   85.1ms     11.1     6.21MB     25.8
#> 2 base         95.1ms  137.2ms      6.98   781.3KB     26.1
```

<sup>Created on 2026-03-20 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

This approach could very well be extended to other iterating functions, like `every()` or maybe `reduce()` from another of my PRs. Or even `pmap()`, because I've decided it looks too complicated to try it now, but it could save a lot of time potentially, as it takes more arguments. I also decided that `map2()` should use faster route only when both `x` and `y` are vectors, but it can be extended to cover mixed cases where only one is an object, too.

title: Speed up the map family
description:
## Summary

This reworks the C implementation of the `map()`, `map2()`, and `pmap()` families to remove repeated R evaluation and other per-element overhead while preserving S3 extraction, coercion, progress, interrupt, and indexed-error behavior.

## Changes and motivation

- Pass input vectors directly to the C implementations. Bare vectors are read through cached read-only data pointers; objects still use `[[` so S3/vctrs dispatch is preserved. This removes repeated evaluation of `.x[[i]]` and `.y[[i]]` in R.
- Build one reusable call per map invocation and update its argument cells directly. Symbols and language objects are quoted before insertion so they continue to be passed as data. This avoids per-element environment rebinding and symbol lookup.
- Omit `...` from the reusable call when it is empty. Empty dots previously incurred expansion overhead on every iteration.
- Resolve `.f` once and place the function directly in the reusable call. This avoids resolving the callback for every element.
- Allow mapped arguments to remain lazy. Because calls now contain the actual extracted values rather than references to a changing loop binding, callbacks can safely force only the arguments they use. This particularly helps `map2()` and `pmap()` callbacks that ignore some inputs.
- Skip all cli progress setup and volatile timer polling when `.progress = FALSE`. Explicit progress bars retain the existing path.
- Add direct output paths. List results go straight to `SET_VECTOR_ELT()` without redundant protection, and exact-type atomic results write through a cached output pointer. Results needing coercion retain `set_vector_value()`.
- Construct `pmap()` argument and S3 extraction machinery once per invocation rather than rebuilding nested subset calls per element.
- Add the `VECTOR_PTR_RO()` compatibility definition needed before R 4.5.

The internal call shown by `sys.call()` now contains the resolved function and mapped values. That representation is an implementation detail; the test now checks the meaningful call properties rather than its exact syntax.

## Performance

`bench::mark()` medians for 10,000 elements, compared with purrr 1.2.2 on R 4.5 / Apple arm64:

| Workload | purrr 1.2.2 | This PR | Improvement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `map(list, identity)` | 1.669 ms | 1.003 ms | 40% |
| `map_int(integer, identity)` | 1.810 ms | 1.096 ms | 39% |
| `map_dbl(double, identity)` | 1.813 ms | 1.096 ms | 40% |
| `map2_int(integer, integer, add)` | 3.192 ms | 1.814 ms | 43% |
| two-argument `pmap_int()` | 4.187 ms | 1.856 ms | 56% |
| five-argument `pmap_int()` | 9.293 ms | 3.907 ms | 58% |

The first direct-extraction/call changes account for most of the gain. In isolated comparisons against that faster intermediate implementation, the later changes improve callbacks using only a subset of arguments by roughly 10–17%; callbacks forcing every argument improve by roughly 3–8%.

## Verification

- 1,032 tests pass.
- Existing coverage exercises symbolic inputs, retained closures, S3/vctrs extraction, coercion, dots forwarding, progress bars, interrupts, and indexed errors.
- `git diff --check` passes.

title: Fix deprecated C API for CRAN
description: With the upcoming R 4.6.0, `Rf_findVar()` and `Rf_findVarInFrame()` will be deprecated and raise warnings (like in the currently failing CRAN checks). Starting with R 4.5.0, there are two functions -- `R_getVar()` and `R_getVarEx()` -- that are meant to replace them, as per "Writing R Extensions": The difference is that `R_getVar()` raises an error if symbol not found, and `R_getVarEx()` returns a specified default value instead. Since both previous functions returned `R_UnboundValue` if symbol not found, technically, a drop-in replacement would be: | before | after | |---|---| | `Rf_findVar(symbol, env)` | `R_getVarEx(symbol, env, TRUE, R_UnboundValue)` | | `Rf_findVarInFrame(env, symbol)` | `R_getVarEx(symbol, env, FALSE, R_UnboundValue)` | For **cleancall.c** and its extraction of `.Call` though, it's better to use `R_getVar()`, as we would rather get an error if `.Call` is missing (and, honestly, the user would have much more pressing problems if it was indeed missing). I've created a conditional define block in C for R < 4.5.0, since that's when these two new functions were introduced, but defining for R < 4.6.0 would also work. PS. As with all my other PRs, I've updated test snaps to vctrs v0.7.0.

title: Rewrite `every()`, `some()`, and `none()` in C
description:
Fixes #1036 

This PR reimplements `every()`, `some()`, and `none()` in C. I followed the C implementation of `map()` (since I have no experience writing in C). The interface does not change at all, the behaviour should also remain intact.

The key change is I did not use `as_predicate()`, but `as_mapper()` instead. Now, the difference between these two functions is that the former performs a Bool check on its output. This was computationally expensive and even replacing this check with `.Call()` didn't help, since the code was switching between C and R contexts a lot. My final solution was to perform these checks in C, in the same code that performs the predicate-checking loop.

I had to replace the implementation of `none()` with a separate C solution, since `negate()` had a huge overhead. However, all three functions share almost all of their C implementations now.

Finally, the performance. They should be equal now (except that `every()` and friends still have their early return).

``` r
library(purrr)

x <- as.list(1:10000)

fn <- function(x) {
  vctrs::vec_is(x) || is.null(x)
}

# Three basic benchmarks
bench::mark(
  all(map_lgl(x, fn)),
  every(x, fn),
  min_time = 1
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression               min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>          <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 all(map_lgl(x, fn))   15.8ms   16.3ms      59.0    4.15MB     44.3
#> 2 every(x, fn)          15.4ms   16.2ms      59.5   12.16KB     46.5

bench::mark(
  any(map_lgl(x, vctrs::vec_is_list)),
  some(x, vctrs::vec_is_list),
  min_time = 1
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression                             min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                          <bch:> <bch:>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 any(map_lgl(x, vctrs::vec_is_list)) 6.94ms  7.2ms      135.    43.7KB     29.6
#> 2 some(x, vctrs::vec_is_list)         6.79ms 7.09ms      138.     9.7KB     27.5

bench::mark(
  !any(map_lgl(x, is.null)),
  none(x, is.null),
  min_time = 1
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression                     min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 !any(map_lgl(x, is.null))   4.78ms   4.99ms      197.   228.5KB     33.2
#> 2 none(x, is.null)             4.8ms   4.96ms      194.     9.7KB     33.2

# `negate()` has a lot of overhead
bench::mark(
  all(map_lgl(x, negate(is.null))),
  every(x, negate(is.null)),
  min_time = 1
)
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is
#> disabled.
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression                            min  median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>                       <bch:tm> <bch:t>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 all(map_lgl(x, negate(is.null)))    112ms   117ms      8.55    3.26MB     32.3
#> 2 every(x, negate(is.null))           114ms   124ms      7.84    2.67MB     24.5

# An early stop example
bench::mark(
  any(map_lgl(x, is.integer)),

#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression                       min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
```

title: Clear `dim` before calling `list_flatten()`
description:
We plan to release vctrs on Jan 15, and purrr was an affected revdep.

In vctrs, `obj_is_list()` no longer reports `TRUE` for a _list array_.

This is because most vctrs functions such as `list_drop_empty()` and `list_combine()` / `list_unchop()` validate their input using `obj_is_list()`, but they aren't well defined on list arrays. In other words when we say "list" in vctrs we really do mean a vector list, not an array list, and `size` related invariants and C code depend on that definition.

This change has affected `array_branch()`, since _sometimes_ `apply()` would return a list array and _sometimes_ it would return a bare list. I think it returns a list array when you apply over >1 dimensions at once, based on looking at the tests.

I am clearing the `dim` only when it exists, because if you clear the `dim` on a bare list then it also drops its names, and we have some tests that ensure that we _keep_ names when only going over 1 dimension.

title: Implemented S7 by swapping the `rate` class and subclasses from S3
description:
Fixes #1129 

**Notes/caveats:**

I changed some tests to account for the new syntax of S7 objects--eg. changing `$` to `@`. Additionally, the new constructor for `rate` objects is called just `rate()` instead of `new_rate()` so I also changed some variable names in the tests to not conflict with that.

I don't like line 71 in rate.R. There, I have a subclass with a different default value of a property than the parent class. I want to override the super's default value for `max_times`, but when I just include `max_times` as a property of the subclass with a different default, the constructed object's value goes to that of the parent. (3 instead of Infinity for `rate_delay`).

I got around it by checking if `max_times` was supplied as an argument and providing the correct default value if it wasn't.

I didn't write change any documentation, so if that needs to be changed I will fix that. The changes are mainly internal, but it may be good to document what certain things are doing so that if S7 changes the purpose of the code can still be understood.

Mentioning @kbodwin since this PR is part of the awesome Independent Study: Advanced R with Dr Bodwin this quarter!

title: Make `in_parallel()` fall back to sequential if daemons are not set
description:
Closes #1186.

To ease programmatic use of purrr within other (package) functions.

From a developer's perspective, compute should just be performed with whatever resources the user has available. The resources are declared by the `mirai::daemons()` call. If a user has not set this then sequential is the only safe fallback.

The onus is then on the developer to inform users that they *should* be calling `mirai::daemons()` to take advantage of parallel processing.

If the nature of things is that a function should always be run in parallel (or so that users don't easily forget to set daemons), a new function in mirai `mirai::require_daemons()` allows a developer to easily put this check before the map call. This basically replicates the behaviour we have now prior to this PR.

title: Update Parallelization to eliminate the `.parallel` argument
description:
This PR updates the existing parallel implementation by replacing the `.parallel` argument of `map()` functions with the use of `parallelize()` as an alias of `carrier::crate()`.

By requiring `parallelize()` as _the_ way to enable parallel operation, we no longer need to worry about which functions need to be crated or not, or when to perform auto-crating. This also has the added benefit of forcing the use of lambda functions (or formulae), i.e.
```r
map(1:3, stats::rnorm, .parallel = TRUE)
map(1:3,\(x) stats::rnorm(x), .parallel = TRUE)

# Now all become:
map(1:3, parallelize(\(x) stats::rnorm(x)))
```

- The test suite has been updated, and the only changes recorded in the snapshot tests are due to the changes in the calls themselves.
- The main documentation is now included under the definition for `parallelize()`.

Also as discussed, perhaps we want to use the adverb `in_parallel()` rather than `parallelize()` to be semantically clearer. So the above example would become:

```r
map(1:3, in_parallel(\(x) stats::rnorm(x)))
```
I'm happy to make this change if we're in agreeement - just let me know.

title: Parallelized map using mirai
description:
@hadley this builds on the proof of concept you reviewed last week at https://github.com/shikokuchuo/purrr/pull/1.

Adds a `.parallel` argument to every function that currently accepts a `.progress` argument, i.e.:
- `map()` and variants
- `map2()` and variants
- `pmap()` and variants

There is a full test suite added at `test-parallel.R`, which runs parallel versions of __all__ the tests from the map/map2/pmap test files, so I'm fairly confident that the behaviour is consistent.

This version relies on current dev `mirai`. I made certain upstream changes to align, in particular, the error messages so that they are consistent and identical to the normal map cases. I'm ready to make another mirai release once this PR is merged.

I've added a couple of simple examples at the bottom of `map()` so it's hopefully clear to users what they should be doing.

The full documentation is available as an Rd page at `?parallelization`. I've added it this way, as opposed to a vignette, to mirror how `.progress` is documented. It also has the advantage of linking easily from function documentation. This contains:
- An explanation of when to provide a list to `.parallel`
- How to set `daemons()`
- The `with()` method for daemons
---
Conceptually, this has been mostly an interface-mapping exercise, with purrr directly using the public exported functions `mirai_map()` and `collect_mirai()` from the mirai package. I've focused almost completely on consistency with the normal, non-parallel, versions thus far.

I've resisted the urge to do any specific optimization for efficiency, as it's likely premature to do so. Just noting here that this is likely to yield results in future.

Welcome your review!

cc. @jcheng5 FYI.

closes #1162.

Just a suggestion: it is more robust and portable to run this as a `make` step rather than introduce a configure script.

Configure should only be used to query and set platform specific things (which is why you ran into the biarch problem). What you are doing here does not require configure, it is the same on any OS. There is no need to depend on a shell script for it, and you can avoid a lot of issues by not introducing one (many windows users don't have a shell on the PATH, etc).

title: Set `Biarch: true` for old R versions on Windows
description:
Now that we have a `configure.win` script, we are forced to also set `Biarch: true` so that when purrr is installed from source on R < 4.2, it installs for both 32 and 64 bit Windows.

Otherwise, we get failures like this one in tidyr on our Windows 3.6 builds if we request `purrr (>= 1.0.0)`:
https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/actions/runs/3743952288/jobs/6356732834

```
*** arch - i386
Error: Error: package or namespace load failed for 'tidyr' in library.dynam(lib, package, package.lib):
 DLL 'purrr' not found: maybe not installed for this architecture?
```

This doesn't happen on newer versions of R because R 4.2 dropped support for 32 bit Windows. This is why windows-latest passes on tidyr.

See 6.3.4 of https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-patched/R-admin.html for more details.

```
Windows
where there is a non-empty configure.win script, or a file src/Makefile.win (with some exceptions where the package is known to have an architecture-independent configure.win, or if --force-biarch or field ‘Biarch’ in the DESCRIPTION file is used to assert so).

In those cases only the current architecture is installed.
```

This might be important enough for a patch purrr release.

title: Rework flattening
description:
This is a large PR that reworks flattening, removing inconsistencies and switching to vctrs as a backend. 

The key idea is to introduce a new family of "combining" functions: `list_c()`, `list_rbind()`, and `list_cbind()`, which replace `flatten_lgl()`, `flatten_int()`, `flatten_dbl()`, `flatten_chr()` (now `list_c()`), `flatten_dfc()` (`list_cbind()`), and `flatten_dfr()` (`list_rbind()`). The new functions are straightforward wrappers around vctrs functions, but somehow feel natural in purrr to me. 

This leaves `flatten()`, which had a rather idiosyncratic interface. It's now been replaced by `list_flatten()` which now always removes a single layer of list hierarchy (and nothing else). While working on this I realised that this was actually what `splice()` did, so overall this feels like a major improvement in naming consistency.

With those functions in place we can deprecate `map_dfr()` and `map_dfc()` which are actually "flat" map functions because they combine, rather than simplify, the results. They have never actually belonged with `map_int()` and friends because they don't have the restriction that `.f` needs to return a length-1 results. This also strongly implies that `flat_map()` would just be `map_c()` and is thus not necessary.

* Fixes #376 by deprecating `map_dfc()`
* Fixes #405 by clearly ruling against `map_c()`
* Fixes #472 by deprecating `map_dfr()`
* Fixes #575 by introducing `list_c()`, `list_rbind()`, and `list_cbind()`
* Fixes #757 by deprecating `flatten_dfr()` and `flatten_dfc()`
* Fixes #758 by introducing `list_rbind()` and `list_cbind()`
* Part of #900

----

Updated to reflect that we no longer believe that `_cbind()`, `_rbind()` and `_c()` are necessary as they're very lightweight wrappers.

title: Use vctrs for flattening into atomic vectors
description:
I added a bit of theory in `?flatten` to explain the current flattening semantics.

The new implementation supports vctrs coercions:

```r
# Before
flatten_chr(list("foo", factor("bar")))
#> [1] "foo" "1"

# After
flatten_chr(list("foo", factor("bar")))
#> [1] "foo" "bar"
```

The historical numeric-to-character coercion is still supported (when vctrs coercion fails) but deprecated:

```r
flatten_chr(list("foo", 1))
#> [1] "foo"      "1.000000"
#> Warning message:
#> Numeric to character coercion is deprecated as of purrr 0.4.0.
#> This warning is displayed once per session.
```

The historical behaviour with data frames is preserved:

```r
flatten_dbl(data.frame(x = 1:2, y = 3:4))
#> [1] 1 2 3 4
```

But I wonder if this should be deprecated? In a way this is consistent with how `map()` supports data frames though.

Improves performance. Interestingly vctrs has gotten faster than `unlist()`?

```r
flatten_int_old <- function(.x) {
  .Call(vflatten_impl, .x, "integer")
}
flatten_int_rlang <- rlang::flatten_int

x <- list(1L, 2:10 + 0L, 11:12 + 0L)
bench::mark(
  base = unlist(x, recursive = FALSE),
  vctrs = flatten_int(x),
  old = flatten_int_old(x),
  rlang = flatten_int_rlang(x)
)[1:8]
```

title: Implement `map_vec()`
description:
This PR implements `map_vec()`, a vctrs powered `map()` that attempts to simplify the output automatically by computing the common type of the result elements. If a common type can be found, the result will be simplified to that type. If not, a list is returned.

This is a draft PR for now as I'm not currently proposing that it be merged. I'd like to get feedback and see what others think about it.

- [ ] Add tests
- [ ] Add examples

This function maintains the invariant that:

```
vec_size(.x) == vec_size(map_vec(.x))
```

After glancing at the issues, it seems this PR touches: #679, #633, #472, #376

For now, here are a number of examples that demonstrate the features of `map_vec()`:

<details>

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)
options(rlang_backtrace_on_error = "reminder")

# Auto simplified to an integer vector
map_vec(1:2, ~ .x)
#> [1] 1 2

# Prevent simplification with `.ptype = list()`
map_vec(1:2, ~ .x, .ptype = list())
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 2

# If a `.ptype` is specified, and casting to that type
# is not possible, an error is raised
map_vec(1:2, ~ .x, .ptype = factor())
#> Can't cast <integer> to <factor<>>

# If simplification is possible, all elements must have size 1,
# otherwise an error is raised
map_vec(1:2, ~ if (.x == 1L) 1:2 else 3)
#> Result 1 must be a single double, not an integer vector of length 2

# If you use `.ptype = list()`, this is pseudo-relaxed
# (The size of the output is still the same as the 
# size of the input (2), but each inner element can vary in size)
map_vec(1:2, ~ if (.x == 1L) 1:2 else 3, .ptype = list())
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 3

# The best thing about `map_vec()` is its flexibility with other
# non-atomic types, for example, simplifying to a date vector
map_vec(1:2, ~ Sys.Date() + .x)
#> [1] "2019-06-19" "2019-06-20"

# If a common type cannot be determined, a list is returned
map_vec(list(1, "x"), ~ .x)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "x"

# Note that just because a common type isn't found doesn't mean you
# can't still forcibly cast to a certain type.
map_vec(list(1, "x"), ~ .x, .ptype = character())
#> [1] "1" "x"

# The underlying `vec_c()` engine knows how to combine 
# data frame output, but this isn't a `map_dfr()` replacement
map_vec(1:2, ~ tibble(x = .x))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1     1
#> 2     2

# You can enforce the structure of the data frame output with a ptype.
# This has the same result as before but coerces the integers to characters
ptype <- tibble(x = character())
map_vec(1:2, ~ tibble(x = .x), .ptype = ptype)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>   x    
#>   <chr>
#> 1 1    
#> 2 2

# And this errors
map_vec(1:2, ~ tibble(x = .x, y = 1), .ptype = ptype)
#> Lossy cast from <tbl_df<
#>   x: integer
#>   y: double
#> >> to <tbl_df<x:character>>.
#> Dropped variables: `y`

# Or you can enforce a partial structure with a partial_frame()
# This ensures that a `y` column exists
partial_ptype <- partial_frame(y = numeric())
map_vec(1:2, ~ tibble(x = .x), .ptype = partial_ptype)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>       x     y
#>   <int> <dbl>
#> 1     1    NA
#> 2     2    NA

# Turning on strict mode forces the user to provide a .ptype
withr::with_options(
  list(vctrs.no_guessing = TRUE),
  map_vec(1:5, ~ .x)
)
#> Error: strict mode is activated; you must supply complete `.ptype`.
```

</details>

title: Changes list_modify to be able to remove key-value pairs whose value is a list
description:
The documentation to `list_modify` indicates that one should "[u]se `zap()` to remove values" from a list. This does not work in the expected way when attempting to remove a key-value pair whose value is a list:

```r
library(purrr)

list(foo = 1, bar = 2) %>% list_modify(foo = zap())

list(foo = c(1, 2), bar = 3) %>% list_modify(foo = zap())

list(foo = list(fst = 1, snd = 2), bar = 3) %>% list_modify(foo = zap())
```

The first two examples above return an object identical to `list(bar = 3)`; the third is such that the call to `list_modify` is a no-op. This pull request fixes this behaviour. It also adds a unit test to cover this case.

Issues: #776

title: Fix `compose()` with generics
description:
And expand the test set to cover many edge cases.

I think `compose()` should now be the recommended way of creating function operators. For instance there are many bugs in the current version of `negate()` which doesn't work with generic functions or functions with explicit `return()`. This will all be fixed by using this implementation which also looks much cleaner:

```r
negate <- function(.p) {
  compose(`!`, as_mapper(.p))
}

negate(is.null)
#> <composed>
#> 1. function (x)
#> .Primitive("is.null")(x)
#>
#> 2. function(.x) !.x
#> <bytecode: 0x7fdb02676d28>
#> <environment: 0x7fdb0303ae78>
```

Using `compose()` to create function operators gives all of these for free:

* The signature of the new function matches the signature of the modified function. This means auto-completion in IDEs.
* Nice `print()` method that shows the different steps of the composition.
* Works with generic functions and dispatches correctly to local methods.
* Works with functions that inspect their immediate dynamic environment, for instance with `match.arg()`.
* Works with multiple levels of arguments passed through dots, both by value and by expression.

* New `slowly()` adverb to wait between each call, by default with a constant rate.

* `rate_sleep()` powers `insistently()` and `slowly()`. It takes a rate, computes a waiting time, and waits. It also throws errors if the max number of attempts is reached.

  The first time that `rate_sleep()` is called, it returns immediately after signalling an init condition. If `rate_sleep()` is called again after it has thrown a max attempt error, it then throws an expiration error suggesting to use `rate_reset()` to reset the rate. An insistent function resets the rate each time it is called.

Closes #389.

title: Early termination with done sentinels
description:
This feature is inspired by https://clojuredocs.org/clojure.core/reduced

* Returning a value wrapped in a `done_box()` terminates a reduction early. `done_box()` is implemented here for now but probably should move to rlang as a general purpose sentinel for early termination.

* If the done box is empty, the last value is used instead. This is not useful for `reduce()` since it is equivalent to returning the result-so-far in a done box. However that's useful for `accumulate()`, the result length is 1 element shorter when returning an empty done box.

* `accumulate()` is rewritten in terms of `reduce_impl()`. I found out that `base::Reduce()` performs a simplification step, which is reproduced for compatibility. On the other hand the new `accumulate2()` function does not simplify, as it seems the right default. We should sort this out for the vctrs milestone, I have opened an issue at https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/599.

title: Follow style guide in error messages
Add error conditions
description:
Common parameters of `stop_` functions:

* `x` as first argument, the actual faulty value. This value is used to obtain the actual length or ptype if need.

* An optional `what` argument that is used to introduce the faulty value. It should be capitalised as it starts the error message. For instance supplying `"Object"` (the default) creates an error message starting with `"Object must be"`.

* An optional `arg` argument to specify from which argument name the faulty value comes. It is used to construct the default `what` value, if not supplied. E.g. `` "`.foo` must be..." ``.


Specific parameters:

* `stop_bad_type()` takes expected and actual type as friendly type descriptors. This gives it the necessary flexibility to be a base error type for the other errors.

  ```r
  stop_bad_type(list(), "a quux", actual = "a foobaz", arg = ".foo")
  #> Error: `.foo` must be a quux, not a foobaz
  ```

* `stop_bad_length()` takes `expected_length` and `.recycle` arguments. The parameters are prefixed with `.` when they are not included in the error object. Both these parameters are used to construct appropriate error messages:

  ```r
  stop_bad_length(1:3, 10)
  #> Error: Vector must have length 10, not 3

  stop_bad_length(1:3, 10, .recycle = TRUE, arg = ".foo")
  #> Error: `.foo` must have length 1 or 10, not 3
  ```

* `stop_bad_vector()` takes `expected_ptype`, and `expected_length`. The ptype is used with `friendly_type_of()` and the new `friendly_element_type_of()` function to construct appropriate error messages:

  ```r
  stop_bad_vector(1:3, character(), 10)
  #> Error: Vector must be a character vector of length 10, not an integer vector of length 3

  stop_bad_vector(1, character(), 1)
  #> Error: Vector must be a single string, not a single double

  stop_bad_vector(factor(c("a", "b")), character(), 1)
  #> Error: Vector must be a single string, not a vector of class `factor` and of length 2
  ```

* All these throwers have "element" variants which take an `index` argument. For these variants, `what` describes the container:

  ```r
  stop_bad_element_type(1:3, 1, "a foobaz")
  #> Error: Element 1 must be a foobaz, not an integer vector

  stop_bad_element_length(1:3, 2, expected_length = 1, what = "Index")
  #> Error: Index 2 must have length 1, not 3

  stop_bad_element_vector(1:3, 3, expected_ptype = character(), expected_length = 10, arg = ".foo")
  #> Error: Element 3 of `.foo` must be a character vector of length 10, not an integer vector of length 3
  ```

title: Binary mappings
description:
This adds binary mapping functions.
- `map_pairs()` applies a function over combinations of `.x` generated by `cross_n()`.
- `map_neighbours()` applies a function to all sequential elements of `.x`. This is particularly useful to check that all elements are identical.

This also adds predicate versions of these functions: `probe_`, `every_` and `some_` variants.

One aspect I'm not sure you'll like is that `map_pairs()` uses attributes to record the parents of the returned elements. Otherwise there is no way to know for sure.

title: Chart
description:
Here is a second attempt. The tools implemented in this PR are more general than in #41 and hopefully correspond to what you had in mind for #9.
- There is a mapping functional `map_along()` that applies a function on a sequence of subsets of a list `.x`. The sequence is controlled by `.route`, which can be a list of indices or a function that takes `.x` and returns a sequence.
  
  I added two such functions, `seq_window()` and `seq_pairs()`. The first can be used to generate indices for a sliding window, while the latter uses `cross()` to generate pairs of indices.
- `chart()` is like `map_along()` but it is a factory that transforms a function that takes a list to apply it on a given route (a given sequence of indices). This way we have a factory and a functional that serve the same purpose, just like `map_call()` and `stitch()`.
- I also added a type predicate `is_index()` to test if an atomic vector can be used as indices (i.e., it tests if a vector is either character or numeric).

title: Enhancements to flatten()
description:
This adds a `.unname` argument to `flatten()`. The goal is to avoid parasite names such as in the following example:

``` r
l <- list(A = list(a = 1, b = 2), B = list(c = 3, d = 4))
flatten(l) %>% str()
## List of 4
##  $ A.a: num 1
##  $ A.b: num 2
##  $ B.c: num 3
##  $ B.d: num 4
```

With `.unname = TRUE`, this becomes:

``` r
flatten(l, .unname = TRUE) %>% str()
## List of 4
##  $ a: num 1
##  $ b: num 2
##  $ c: num 3
##  $ d: num 4
```

The unnaming behavior differs as a function of `.recursive`: with recursive flattening, `unlist()` is called with `use.names = FALSE`. In the non-recursive case, only the names of the outer list are zapped.

This also makes `flatten(list())` return an empty list instead of `NULL` as suggested in #58.

title: Rename smash() to stitch() and implement smash()

This implements a complement to `smash()`, ie a functional that transforms a function taking a list into a variadic function.

While I was thinking about a name for that new functional, I realised we got the analogy backwards. I think `smash()` would better be called `stitch()` and the new functional should be called `smash()` instead. The smash analogy would work better with this functional because the transformed function goes from one tidy entry point to many ones.

On the other hand, if we transform a function that takes many arguments into one that takes a list, we `stitch()` its function signature into one piece :-)

This is a refactor of the rows-based functionals.
- Part of the functions are rewritten in C, so that we can use `Rf_eval()` and avoid the overhead of `Rcpp_eval()`. This is done by reusing the C implementations of `map()` and `pmap()`.
- `map_rows()` is renamed to `invoke_rows()`. I think this is a better analogy for that function since it works like applying `invoke()` to each row.

- Add `.to` option to change the name of the output column, as per @jennybc's request.

title: Deprecate dataframe-based mapping functions
description:
Deprecation of rows-based functions now that we have the new mapping functions in dplyr and the nest() / mutate() / map() idiom.

One use case that does not have any equivalent in dplyr is when the output is within the range `c(1, nrow(df))`. For example:

``` r
dmap(mtcars, summary)
```

This can be worked around, for example here we'd do

``` r
mtcars %>% map(summary) %>% as_data_frame()
```

However a new dplyr family of verbs for variable-length output may be useful. It could be called `condense()`.
- Like `summarise()` it would discard all input columns except for the grouping variables. This allows the output to have a different number of rows than the input.
- Unlike `summarise()`, it would not require length 1 results and would only check for equal length within group. Grouping columns would be recycled to these lengths.

Ungrouped data frame: check squared constraint

``` r
mtcars %>% condense(col = 1:5, other = 5:1)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>     col other
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1     5
#> 2     2     4
#> 3     3     3
#> 4     4     2
#> 5     5     1

mtcars %>% condense(col = 1:5, other = 2:1)
#> Error: results must have same length
```

This gives us immediately:

``` r
mtcars %>% condense_all(summary)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 11
#>           mpg         cyl        disp          hp        drat
#>   <S3: table> <S3: table> <S3: table> <S3: table> <S3: table>
#> 1        10.4        4.00        71.1        52.0        2.76
#> 2        15.4        4.00       121.0        96.5        3.08
#> 3        19.2        6.00       196.0       123.0        3.70
#> 4        20.1        6.19       231.0       147.0        3.60
#> 5        22.8        8.00       326.0       180.0        3.92
#> 6        33.9        8.00       472.0       335.0        4.93
#> # ... with 6 more variables: wt <S3: table>, qsec <S3: table>, vs <S3:
#> #   table>, am <S3: table>, gear <S3: table>, carb <S3: table>
```

For a grouped data frame, we'd check the square constrain within groups:

``` r
grouped <- mtcars %>% group_by(am)

grouped %>%
  condense(
    col = rep(mean(cyl), times = round(mean(cyl))),
    other = rep(length(col), length(col))
  )
#> # A tibble: 12 x 3
#>       am   col other
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1      0  6.95     7
#> 2      0  6.95     7
#> 3      0  6.95     7
#> 4      0  6.95     7
#> 5      0  6.95     7
#> 6      0  6.95     7
#> 7      0  6.95     7
#> 8      1  5.08     5
#> 9      1  5.08     5
#> 10     1  5.08     5
#> 11     1  5.08     5
#> 12     1  5.08     5

grouped %>%
  condense(
    col = rep(mean(cyl), times = round(mean(cyl))),
    other = rep(length(col), length(col) - 1)
  )
#> Error: results must have same length within groups
```

title: Fix outdated version number

That one was a "maintenance release following the release of dplyr 0.7.5", which I guess came in though some other pipeline than the "normal" GitHub path.

I noticed this as I ran into the bug reported in #429 (parameter `.id` is ignored in `imap_dfr()`), for which a fix was merged on Feb 5 in #454. However, while this fix is on the current master branch (0.2.4.9000), it is not included in CRAN's 0.2.5.

The result is that I cannot make my package depend on the fixed version, as 0.2.5 > 0.2.4.9000.

This PR hence bumps the version number on GitHub from 0.2.4.9000 to 0.2.5.9000. Then it is possible to make another package depend on purrr 0.2.5.9000, which does include the needed fix.

title: Added create_env
description:
This can help people dealing with the issue at https://github.com/hadley/tidyr/issues/224.

Adds create_env and in_new_env.

Typical usage would be something like:

```
# More explicit what;s going on
list(iris_new_env = iris) %>% 
  create_env() %>% 
  with({
    lm(Sepal.Width ~ Sepal.Length, iris_new_env)
  })

# and simpler syntax:
in_new_env(lm)(Sepal.Width ~ Sepal.Length, iris_new_env)
```

And here it is in action fixing the above issue:

```
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
iris_big <- iris %>% as.tbl() %>%  
  mutate(iris = rep(list(iris), NROW(.)))

iris_big3 <- iris_big %>% 
  mutate(plot = iris %>% map(function(x){
    Seatbelts_big <- Seatbelts %>% data.frame() %>% as.tbl() %>%  
      mutate(Seatbelts = rep(list(Seatbelts), NROW(.))) 
    # Now use the new function
    list(x = x) %>% 
      create_env() %>% 
      with({
        x %>% ggplot(aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) + geom_point()
      })
  }))

# Size in memory is reasonable (but when calling this using multidplyr it isn't)
object.size(iris_big3)
#2759016 bytes
save(iris_big3, file = "tmp.RData")
file.size("tmp.RData")
# Size on disk is now correct.
#77221 (3% of memory used)

# And similarly with in_new_env:
iris_big3 <- iris_big %>% 
  mutate(plot = iris %>% map(function(x){
    Seatbelts_big <- Seatbelts %>% data.frame() %>% as.tbl() %>%  
      mutate(Seatbelts = rep(list(Seatbelts), NROW(.))) 
    # Now use the new function
    in_new_env(ggplot)(x, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) + geom_point()
  }))

```

title: Implement probe()
description:
`probe(x, predicate)` is a shortcut meant to be the equivalent to `map_v(x, predicate, .type = logical(1))`.

The need for such a shortcut is somewhat compensated by all lowliner functions taking a predicate as argument: `keep()`, `map_if()`, ... However there are still situations where it is needed to construct a logical vector.

For example, if we use `map_if()` twice to selectively modify the list when a predicate is TRUE and an alternative modification when it's FALSE, we need to record such a logical vector because the contents of the list are altered during the first `map_if()` call. Example:

```
l <- list(a = 1, b = "2", c = "3")

is_character <- probe(l, is.character)
l <- l %>%
  map_if(is_character, as.numeric) %>%
  map_if(!is_character, as.character)
```

I think `probe()` would be a nice little touch of sugar and make the code a bit more expressive in these situations.

title: Data frame coercion in multi maps
description:
This patch fixes my PR of yesterday so that `map2()` and `map3()` coerce their outputs to a data frame they get one as input. I added some tests to check we don't break this again in the future. However I'm not sure what to do about `map_n()`. Since the result is never a named list, it can never be coerced by `as_data_frame()`. Non-exclusive possibilities to solve this:
1. Never coerce to a data frame (don't use the output hook).
2. Coerce to a data frame based on the first element of `.l`. This may be a good option because the behavior would be symmetric with `map2()` and `map3()`. This would simplify the code as well (no need of `map_multi()`).
3. Add names automatically. That's what I did in a recent commit pushed to #24. This was to make `cross()` not fail when given a data frame with `.wide = TRUE`. In retrospective I'm not sure this is a good thing, and in any case this should be handled by `as_data_frame()` not by lowliner.
4. Downcast to a list when data frame coercion is not possible (i.e., when the list is not named or when its elements have unequal lengths).

I think 2 and 4 would be nice.

title: Let splat() specify default arguments for .f
description:

When we pipe a list into a splatted function, it is often necessary to take care of additional arguments. That typically means adjusting the main list with additional arguments by using a temporary variable or `append()`ing  them in the middle of the pipe chain. Being able to specify these arguments directly in `splat()` hopefully leads to clearer code because the main arguments and the side arguments are specified separately (the former in the pipe chain and the latter in `splat()`).

title: Implement at_depth()
description:
While writing the PR I noticed that `at_depth()` is basically a recursive version of `map()`, not necessarily an adverb for functions that take a list. So now I find it a bit odd that it is not called something like `map_at_depth()` (but I don't think I like this name). 

Also, the semantics is not great when the list is not piped. e.g.,

```
list %>% at_depth(3, sum)  # looks good
at_depth(list, 3, sum)     # looks odd
```

So from this point of view maybe the idea of a factory function is better:

```
list %>% at_depth(3, sum)()
at_depth(3, sum)(list)
```
